ai.definition: Digital Afterlife is a speculative technology aimed at preserving and transferring human consciousness into a digital format after death.
ai.howItWorks: This involves creating highly advanced neural interfaces capable of reading brain activity and mapping it to a digital environment. AI techniques are then used to simulate the consciousness based on this data, potentially enabling an upload or transfer into a virtual space.
ai.problemSolved: The technology addresses the existential concern of human consciousness ceasing upon death by offering a means to preserve it in a digital form for potential future reanimation or existence.
ai.manufacturing: Current manufacturing processes are at a conceptual stage, with no practical implementation. Development would require breakthroughs in neural interface technology and AI capabilities.
ai.buildProcess: Building the infrastructure for a digital afterlife involves developing non-invasive or minimally invasive brain-computer interfaces, advanced machine learning algorithms to interpret brain signals, and robust virtual environments capable of supporting simulated consciousness.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include research and development in neural interface technology, AI advancements, and the creation of complex virtual ecosystems. Initial costs are likely to be extremely high due to cutting-edge nature.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is highly speculative with significant technical challenges but potential for long-term societal impact if successful.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations currently exist, making it a largely unregulated field. However, ethical and legal frameworks will need to be developed as the technology matures.
ai.risks: Risks include technological limitations in accurately mapping consciousness, ethical concerns around the nature of simulated existence, potential misuse or abuse of the technology, and societal implications of offering digital immortality.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to speculative nature and high initial costs. If successful, it could potentially generate significant revenue through subscription models for virtual environments or services.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving neural interface accuracy, enhancing AI capabilities to better simulate consciousness, and creating more immersive virtual realities.

glossary.def: A device that can read or stimulate the nervous system for medical, therapeutic, or technological purposes.
A subset of artificial intelligence that involves training algorithms to make predictions or decisions based on data without being explicitly programmed.
A computer-generated simulation of a three-dimensional environment that can be interacted with in a seemingly real or physical way through specialized equipment like headsets or gloves.

subsystems.name: Preservation
subsystems.role: stabilises a brain so its wiring survives long enough to be read.

subsystems.name: Imaging
subsystems.role: captures every neuron, axon and synapse at nanometre resolution.

subsystems.name: Reconstruction
subsystems.role: turns petabytes of images into a wiring diagram.

subsystems.name: Physiological model
subsystems.role: adds dynamics to the wiring — how each cell actually behaves.

subsystems.name: Simulation substrate
subsystems.role: runs the model fast enough to behave in real time.

subsystems.name: Validation and interface
subsystems.role: checks the model against real brains and gives it senses and outputs.
parts: comparison with electrode and imaging recordings

buildSteps.title: Preserve the tissue
buildSteps.detail: A donor brain would be perfused with fixatives or cryoprotectants within minutes of death, then vitrified and stored cold to stop decay before imaging.

buildSteps.title: Cut and image
buildSteps.detail: The brain is sliced into nanometre-thin sections and each is photographed by electron microscopy, producing petabytes of images over months to years.

buildSteps.title: Segment the images
buildSteps.detail: Machine-learning models trace every cell membrane and process; human proofreaders fix errors, as done for small animal connectomes.

buildSteps.title: Map the synapses
buildSteps.detail: Each junction is located and classified by type and strength, giving a directed graph of perhaps 10^14 to 10^15 connections in a human brain.

buildSteps.title: Assign cell types
buildSteps.detail: Each neuron is matched to a known type with its ion channels, receptors and firing behaviour — much of this is still unknown for humans.

buildSteps.title: Build the simulation
buildSteps.detail: The graph and cell models are loaded onto a supercomputer, with numerical integration of each neuron's electrical state.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate against real data
buildSteps.detail: Simulated responses are tuned until they match recordings from living tissue; without this the model is a diagram, not a mind.

buildSteps.title: Run and interface
buildSteps.detail: The emulation is run continuously and connected to sensors and actuators so it can interact with the world.

prerequisites.why: complete connectomes exist only for very small brains; a human brain is roughly a million times larger in volume.
segmentation still needs heavy human proofreading, which does not scale to a human brain.
real-time simulation of tens of billions of detailed neurons needs far more compute and bandwidth than any machine today.
we lack a complete catalogue of human cell types, their channels and how synapses change with learning.

prerequisites.tech: A validated test of mind simulation
prerequisites.why: there is no agreed way to show that a simulation is conscious or is the same person, not merely similar.

pathway.milestone: complete wiring maps of tiny brains (the nematode in 1986, the adult fruit fly in 2024) and partial maps of mouse cortex
pathway.unlocks: proof that connectomes can be read, plus tooling for segmentation and annotation.

pathway.milestone: a whole mouse brain connectome and simulation of small circuits that reproduces real behaviour
pathway.unlocks: methods that could be scaled, and evidence about how much detail behaviour requires.

pathway.milestone: high-resolution maps of human brain tissue, or non-destructive scanning fine enough to resolve synapses
pathway.unlocks: the raw data a human emulation would need — and raises consent and privacy questions.

pathway.milestone: a human-scale emulation running in real time and passing behavioural tests
pathway.unlocks: only then could digital preservation be discussed as a technology rather than a hope.
